claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains intrinsic crystallographic defects.
The bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A regression model using electronic-structure, defect-density, and oxygen-concentration descriptors will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy relative to conventional analytical models.
The proposed improvement will apply in the 0–200 K regime.
The proposed improvement will apply in the 300–1200 K regime.
Electrical scattering at 0–200 K is dominated by defects and impurities.
Electrical scattering at 300–1200 K is governed by phonon and impurity effects.
Crystallographic defects and oxygen impurity sites act as electron-scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Descriptors of defects and oxygen allow the model to adjust temperature-dependent scattering rates.
Accounting for defect- and oxygen-dependent scattering will make predictions better reflect experimental samples than predictions based on defect-free crystals.
Predicted conductivity will be within approximately 20% of experiment in the 0–200 K regime.
Predicted conductivity will be within approximately 20% of experiment in the 300–1200 K regime.
Existing analytical conductivity models are derived from perfect, defect-free crystal assumptions.
Defect-free analytical predictions have larger discrepancies from experiment than the proposed model is expected to have.
Existing analytical models systematically overestimate or underestimate conductivity in real HfNbTaTiZr samples.
The proposed approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The approach is valid only in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Prediction-error variability may arise from variation among experimental datasets and difficulty quantifying defects and impurities.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant error reduction greater than 20% relative to an analytical baseline in at least one temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies an absolute error of about 20% or less in both regimes, whereas the falsification rule tests a greater-than-20% relative improvement over analytical models. These are different benchmarks, so the stated falsification rule does not decisively test the quantified predicted outcome.
